title: Validator‑Guided Repair on a Shared Initial LLM Candidate: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation for Network Configuration Safety
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study to test whether a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline changes the executability of LLM‑produced network configurations when the same single sampled candidate per intent is deterministically reused across baseline and guarded arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Using a declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) the adapter produced one shared initial generation per intent (N=200 pairs; completed_episode_count = 400; model_calls_used = 200). Every shared candidate passed validator checks, so no repairs were applied (repair_attempt_count = 0; repair_applied_count = 0). Observed outcomes: baseline_success_count = 200/200, guarded_success_count = 200/200; paired contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap (seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0]. We provide artifact‑grounded accounting, representative validator traces, and a focused discussion of how shared_initial_candidate semantics constrain causal interpretation. We close with concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations and precise follow‑on preregistered designs to evaluate repair efficacy under independent sampling and higher‑difficulty or adversarial scenarios.

sections.introduction:
LLMs are being explored for intent→configuration workflows in network operations (NetOps). Generated configurations that contain syntactic errors, logical violations (e.g., breaking redundancy constraints), or hallucinated fields present operational risks when executed. Generate–validate–repair (GVR) architectures—where generation is followed by a deterministic validator and optional automated repair—are widely proposed as mitigations in related domains (IaC, program repair). However, the causal conclusions one can draw about GVR depend critically on experimental sampling semantics: if each arm receives independent first‑pass samples, differences may reflect both generation variability and repair; if a single sampled candidate is shared across arms (shared_initial_candidate), any effect must come solely from downstream validation/repair applied to that same candidate. This paper reports a fully preregistered paired confirmatory evaluation (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01) that executed the shared_initial_candidate estimand and produced artifacted deterministic validator traces and complete analysis files.

Research question and contribution. Our preregistered primary question was: does applying a deterministic validator plus one automated repair to a fixed single LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics) change the rate of validator‑valid executable configurations relative to reusing the same candidate without validation/repair? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, reproducible paired experiment executed on N=200 paired intents with complete accounting and archived artifacts; (2) a transparent, artifact‑grounded report showing a degenerate null paired effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics and quantified inferential results; (3) precise operational recommendations and preregistration patterns for future studies that target repair efficacy under sampling variability.
sections.related_work: Prior literature documents hallucination and reference unreliability in LLMs and motivates evidence‑grounded generation and post‑generation verification across domains. Surveys and empirical studies identify hallucination as a central trust problem for operational usage and recommend grounding or verification [1,2]. Retrieval‑augmented and evidence‑grounded pipelines can reduce hallucination in operations‑style QA tasks but do not directly measure device‑level executability in packet‑level simulators [2]. Verifier‑guided approaches and generate–validate–repair pipelines have shown empirical improvements for infrastructure‑as‑code and program‑generation tasks (e.g., TerraFormer and related verifier feedback systems), demonstrating that verifier feedback can reduce incorrect generated artifacts in those domains, though direct device‑execution evaluations are less common in the supplied corpus [3]. NetOps evaluations with LLMs have focused on intent translation and capability measurement; standardized execution‑level safety benchmarks in packet‑level simulators remain a methodological gap that motivated our preregistered experiment [4]. This work situates itself as a narrowly scoped, artifact‑grounded confirmatory test of validator/repair effects under explicitly shared sampling semantics rather than an evaluation of cross‑model generality or deployment readiness.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01) before any model calls. The primary estimand is the paired difference in proportions of validator‑valid executable configurations between guarded (validator + ≤1 repair) and baseline (no validator/repair) under shared_initial_candidate execution. The paired design fixed task_count = 200 and permitted at most one automated repair per guarded episode. The primary test was the exact two‑sided McNemar test on the 2×2 paired contingency table; the analysis also reports a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). The preregistration specified contamination detection, missingness handling, and sensitivity analyses (complete_pair_primary plus a failure‑as‑zero sensitivity mapping).

Task generation, selection, and contamination checks. A deterministic task generator produced a fixed manifest of 200 synthetic 'intent_configuration_repair_v1' intents. Each manifest entry includes initial_state, required_sequence, difficulty annotations, and a generation_seed to enable deterministic replay of the test bank. Contamination checks were preregistered (exact SHA256 match and high‑similarity n‑gram thresholds) and ran prior to execution; no exact‑match exclusions were flagged and no items were removed from the confirmatory sample. Representative manifest fields (intent text, required_sequence, and difficulty patterns such as "safe_access_service_transfer" or "rolling_access_vlan_migration") are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Generation semantics and model configuration. Execution adhered to shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded episodes. The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini via a hosted adapter; the archived execution/model_configuration.json records that temperature = null (unset). We explicitly note that temperature = null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0; nondeterministic sampling remains possible. The adapter produced hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and the adapter audit recorded a single stage labeled shared_initial_generation = 200, consistent with the preregistered sampling semantics.

Validator and automated repair pipeline. Scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with the scoring_rule 'full_intent_constraint_validation' to produce binary executable/invalid labels. For guarded episodes the pipeline was permitted a single automated repair attempt (preregistered maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the baseline reused the same sampled candidate without repair; the guarded arm could alter that same candidate only via the single permitted repair if the validator flagged violations. All validator traces (validation_before and validation_after) and repair metadata are archived per‑episode in execution/scoring/*.json.

Analysis plan and reproducibility mapping. The primary analysis followed the preregistration: exact McNemar two‑sided test for the paired contingency table plus paired bootstrap percentile CI (seed and resample counts as above). Missingness policy used the complete_pair_primary rule: exclude incomplete pairs from primary analysis. All analysis artifacts (paired contingency table, condition summary, missingness summary, contamination summary) and the execution manifest are archived; key artifact paths include execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/scoring/, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, and analysis/condition_summary.csv. The archived artifacts contain the raw LLM responses, validator traces, repair trace placeholders (if any), and the final per‑episode binary scores.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The adapter executed the preregistered plan to completion: planned_episode_count = 400, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0. Because one shared initial generation per pair was produced and reused, model_calls_used = 200 (one model call per pair). The analysis missingness summary reports complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes.

Primary outcomes and inferential results. Baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 per condition). The paired contingency table observed: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) yields a paired difference 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0]. These numeric results and the CSV artifacts are archived under analysis/. The paired table is summarized in Table 1.

Repair activity and representative validator diagnostics. No repairs were attempted or applied in the guarded arm because all shared initial candidates passed validator checks: repair_attempt_count = 0 and repair_applied_count = 0 across the confirmatory sample. Representative per‑episode JSON scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task‑000004‑baseline.json and task‑000004‑guarded.json, task‑000005, task‑000006, etc.) show identical shared_initial_candidate text and identical validator.validation_after.normalized_configuration values for baseline and guarded. Representative shared initial content for a hard task (task‑000004) is: "interface edge2 admin down\ninterface edge2 vlan 40\ninterface edge2 admin up\ninterface edge1 admin down"; the same text appears in both baseline and guarded response files for that pair. Table 2 lists representative per‑episode diagnostics and Table 3 provides the one‑line repair summary (repair_attempt_count and repair_applied_count).

Missingness, contamination, and deterministic reconciliation. Preexecution contamination checks flagged no exact‑match leaks; the analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty. Deterministic reconciliation confirms consistent episode accounting and reports cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false; the provider audit shows cache_miss_count = 200 consistent with fresh shared initial generation for each pair. All deterministic consistency checks passed and are archived in analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json.

Statistical interpretation. The observed degenerate contingency table with zero discordant pairs implies the test statistics (McNemar p = 1.0 and bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]) correctly represent the executed estimand but are uninformative about potential repair efficacy under alternative sampling semantics. Because no validator‑detectable faults were produced in the single sampled candidates, there was no opportunity for repair to change outcomes. This is an artifact‑grounded null result about the specific estimand executed rather than evidence that GVR pipelines are unnecessary more generally.
sections.discussion:
Causal meaning under shared_initial_candidate semantics. By design, shared_initial_candidate semantics hold the sampled generation constant across conditions so that any paired difference must come from downstream validation/repair. In our run every shared candidate was validated as executable; consequently the guarded pipeline could not change outcomes. This narrow causal conclusion is fully supported by the archived provider audit (one shared_initial_generation stage), the per‑episode scoring JSONs showing identical shared candidate text for both conditions, and the recorded repair counts.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) limit internal causal claims to validator/repair effects on the same candidate and preclude sampling variability as a source of discordance. Construct validity: the deterministic validator enforces syntactic and workflow constraints mapped from intent, but it abstracts vendor CLI behavior and does not execute on live devices; vendor‑specific idiosyncrasies or dynamic runtime interactions are therefore not represented. External validity: a single declared model/provider (gpt‑5‑mini via the hosted adapter), a synthetic task bank, and a validator abstraction restrict generalization beyond the studied scope. Conclusion validity: the absence of discordant pairs leaves no empirical basis in this run to estimate repair efficacy under independent sampling; a different preregistered estimand is required to study that question.

Operational implications and recommendations. The run validates an artifacted evaluation pipeline (preregistration, provider audit, deterministic validator traces, and reproducible analysis) that can be used for stronger tests of GVR efficacy. Artifact‑grounded follow‑on designs we recommend (each requires new preregistration and alters the estimand): (1) independent per‑condition first‑pass samples (remove shared_initial_candidate semantics) so that differences can arise from both generation variability and repair; (2) targeted high‑difficulty and adversarial task subsets to increase expected discordant pairs; (3) explicit sampling‑parameter sweeps (set temperature to concrete numeric values rather than leaving it null/unset) and record them in model_configuration.json; (4) multi‑model, multi‑provider samples to test generality; and (5) raise validator fidelity by incorporating vendor CLI semantics or packet‑level emulation to test repairs against dynamic runtime behavior. Each change is recommended because it transforms the estimand and creates the conditions under which repairs can empirically affect paired outcomes.

Representative diagnostics and why artifacts matter. The archived per‑task JSONs provide concrete diagnostics (normalized_configuration, validator.valid flags, validation_before/after subtables, and repair_applied indicators) that make transparent why the paired difference is zero in this run. For reviewers and future experimenters the presence of raw responses, scoring JSONs, the task manifest, and the analysis CSVs allows independent reanalysis of the same estimand without ambiguity about sampling semantics.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory experiment designed to measure validator/repair effects when the same single LLM candidate per intent is reused across baseline and guarded conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics). With gpt‑5‑mini as the declared generator and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the scorer, every shared initial candidate passed validation and no repairs were attempted or applied; therefore guarded and baseline outcomes were identical on the executed estimand (paired difference = 0.0; McNemar p = 1.0; bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]). This result is evidence‑grounded and narrowly scoped: it speaks only to the downstream effect of validation/repair on the exact sampled candidates produced under the executed sampling semantics and model settings, not to the broader question of whether GVR pipelines reduce misconfiguration rates under independent sampling or other operational regimes. Follow‑on preregistered experiments that change generation semantics (independent per‑condition sampling), increase task difficulty, explicitly set sampling parameters, diversify models/providers, and increase validator fidelity are required to test repair efficacy under realistic sampling variability and adversarial conditions. Our artifacts and pipeline are archived to enable such follow‑on confirmatory designs and independent verification of the executed estimand and results.

limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single sampled initial generation was reused across baseline and guarded conditions; this design measures validator/repair effects only and cannot detect differences caused by independent per‑condition sampling or prompt engineering.

Temperature unset (temperature = null) in the archived model configuration: null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0; sampling nondeterminism may still have occurred during the single sampled generation.
Single model and single hosted provider: results reflect gpt‑5‑mini under the archived adapter; generalization to other models or model families is unsupported by these artifacts.

Synthetic task bank and validator abstraction: tasks were synthetic 'intent_configuration_repair_v1' items and the deterministic validator is an abstraction; realistic vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, emergent runtime interactions, and hardware effects were not executed on live devices.

No observed validator failures: all initial candidates were validator‑valid, so the experiment could not assess the repair step's effectiveness; the null effect therefore reflects the task bank and sampling semantics rather than evidence that GVR is unnecessary in general.
